lessons.title: Verbal reasoning: the True / False / Cannot Say method
lessons.summary: You will be able to classify every statement as True, False or Cannot Say with a fixed decision rule, without falling into the traps of assumptions and outside knowledge.

sections.body:
In SHL- or Kenexa-style verbal reasoning tests you receive a passage of 150-300 words (economics, business, society) and 3-4 statements to assess. For each one you choose one of three answers:

- **True**: the statement follows from the passage.
- **False**: the passage contradicts it.
- **Cannot Say**: the passage does not give enough information to say either True or False.

The average time is about 40-60 seconds per statement, including reading the passage (the exact pace depends on the test provider). These tests do not measure how much you know about finance, but how rigorous you are in separating **what the text says** from **what you think**.

**Note**: some critical thinking tests (e.g. the Watson-Glaser format) use different scales, such as “probably true”. The method in this lesson applies to the three-answer format, the most common in banking graduate programmes.

Treat the passage as **the only truth in the world**, even if it contains things you know to be false. Then ask these questions, in this order:

1. **Find the point in the passage** that the statement refers to.
2. **Does the passage make the statement necessarily true?** That is: if the whole passage is true, is it impossible for the statement to be false? If yes → **True**.
3. **Does the passage make the statement necessarily false?** That is: does it say, or inevitably imply, the opposite? If yes → **False**.
4. **Otherwise** → **Cannot Say**.

| Situation | Answer |
|---|---|
| The text says it, even in different words | True |
| The text implies it without needing additional assumptions | True |
| The text says the opposite or something incompatible | False |
| The text does not mention it | Cannot Say |
| The text mentions it, but concluding requires an assumption | Cannot Say |

The most important row is the fourth: **“not mentioned” does not mean False**. To answer False you need an explicit or logically inevitable contradiction.

As an analyst you know a lot about markets, and in the test that is a risk. If the passage says that “higher rates usually reduce equity multiples” and the statement says “equity multiples fell in 2022”, you may remember that this really happened, but the passage does not say so: **Cannot Say**.

The reverse also applies: if the passage states a fact that you know to be wrong in reality, in the test that fact is true.

**Quick test**: ask yourself “am I using a sentence from the passage or something I know?”. If it is the latter, stop.

The only outside knowledge allowed is the ordinary meaning of words and basic logic: if the text says “all subsidiaries met their targets” and mentions an Italian subsidiary, you can conclude that it too met its target.

The most frequent errors come from inferences that seem obvious but are not necessary. The five most common:

- **Possibility vs certainty**: “may”, “could”, “is expected to”, “plans to” do not become “will” or “did”.
- **Sequence or correlation vs cause**: “after the rate rise, approvals fell” does not say that the rise caused the fall.
- **Part vs whole**: “some”, “many”, “most” say nothing about “all”.
- **Change of period**: “was the market leader in 2019” says nothing about 2025.
- **Change of subject or measure**: the text talks about “revenue”, the statement about “profit”; the text talks about Europe, the statement about Italy.

When the statement is “almost” in the text but with one of these shifts, the correct answer is almost always **Cannot Say**, rarely False.

| In the passage | In the statement | Typical answer |
|---|---|---|
| all / every | some / a specific member of the group | True |
| some / many / most | all | Cannot Say |
| only some / not all / all except X | all | False |
| never / none | sometimes / at least one | False |
| may / could / is likely to | will / does | Cannot Say |
| rose 10% | doubled | False |
| the largest of the group | larger than Y (Y is another member of the group) | True |
| A happened after B | B caused A | Cannot Say |
| X contributed to Y | X was the main cause of Y | Cannot Say |

Two caveats:

- **“Most”** should be treated as “more than half, perhaps all”. You can answer False to a statement with “all” only if the text indicates a specific exception: “not all”, “only some”, “except X”, or a member of the group that does not meet the condition.
- **Double negatives** (“it is not untrue that”) should be rewritten in positive form before you decide.

sections.h: Procedure under time pressure, statement by statement
sections.body:
1. **Read the statement first** and identify subject, verb, number, period and qualifier.
2. **Go to the sentence in the passage** that deals with that subject (see the lesson on fast reading).
3. **Compare element by element**: same subject? same measure? same period? same degree of certainty?
4. **If everything matches** → True. **If one element is incompatible** → False. **If one element is missing or weaker** → Cannot Say.
5. **Do not go back**: once you have decided, move on to the next one.

Final check: to answer **False** you must be able to point to the sentence that contradicts. To answer **True** you must be able to point to the sentence that proves. If you cannot point to either, it is **Cannot Say**.

examples.q: Passage: Northbridge Industrials reported a 12% increase in revenue in 2025, driven mainly by its aerospace division. Each of the three acquisitions it completed during the year was paid entirely in cash. Management expects operating margins to improve in 2026 as raw material costs stabilise. Statement: Northbridge's operating margins will improve in 2026.
steps: Relevant sentence: “Management expects operating margins to improve in 2026”.
The statement turns a management expectation into a certain fact (“will improve”).
The text does not say that margins will improve, nor that they will not: certainty is missing, but there is no contradiction.

examples.q: Same passage. Statement: Northbridge paid for at least one of its 2025 acquisitions partly in shares.
steps: Relevant sentence: “Each of the three acquisitions it completed during the year was paid entirely in cash”.
“Each” covers all three acquisitions and “entirely in cash” rules out any payment in shares, even a partial one.
You can point to the sentence that refutes the statement: a direct contradiction, therefore False.

Watch the change of measure: “paid in cash” concerns the consideration paid to the sellers. If the statement said “the cash was raised through a share issue”, the answer would be Cannot Say, because the text does not say where the cash comes from.

examples.q: Same passage. Statement: Northbridge's revenue was higher in 2025 than in 2024.
steps: Relevant sentence: “a 12% increase in revenue in 2025”, i.e. 2025 revenue = 2024 revenue × 1.12.
If 2025 revenue is 112% of 2024 revenue, it is necessarily higher: no assumption is needed.

examples.q: Passage: In the two years after the central bank of Country X raised its policy rate in 2023, mortgage approvals in the country fell by a third. Statement: The rise in the policy rate caused the fall in mortgage approvals.
steps: The text links the two facts only in time: “In the two years after ... approvals fell”.
The statement adds a causal link (“caused”) that the text does not state.
Your economic knowledge says it is plausible, but the passage neither proves nor rules it out.

cheatsheet: True = follows necessarily from the passage, without assumptions.
False = the passage says the opposite or something incompatible.
Cannot Say = neither proved nor contradicted: it is the default when a piece is missing.
“Not mentioned” is never False.
The passage is the only truth: ignore what you know about the real world.
may / could / expects / plans are not equivalent to will / did.
A time sequence or a correlation is not causation.
some / many / most say nothing about all; only some / not all / except make all False.
For False, point to the sentence that contradicts; for True, the one that proves.

lessons.title: Verbal reasoning: fast reading and keyword matching
lessons.summary: You will be able to find, in a few seconds, the sentence in the passage that decides each statement, without being misled by identical words with a different meaning.

sections.h: The problem is time, not comprehension
sections.body:
You understand every passage without difficulty. The problem is that you have less than a minute per statement and the same passage serves 3-4 statements. If you reread the whole text each time, you lose 20-30 seconds per question and reach the middle of the test with no time left.

Goal of this lesson: **read the passage only once, in a structured way**, then for each statement **go straight to the right sentence**.

Indicative budget for a passage with 4 statements (about 3-4 minutes in total, i.e. 40-60 seconds per statement):

| Phase | Time |
|---|---|
| First read with a mental map | 40-50 s |
| Each statement (keywords, search, check) | 30-40 s |
| Reserve for difficult cases | 10-20 s |

sections.h: First read: the map of the passage
sections.body:
Read the passage once at a brisk pace, without memorising the details. You only need to know **where** everything is:

- **One label per paragraph** (e.g. “P1 revenue, P2 acquisitions, P3 outlook”).
- **Numbers, dates and proper names**: you do not memorise them, you only remember which paragraph they are in.
- **Signal words**, i.e. the points where the answers are decided:

| Type | Words |
|---|---|
| Contrast | however, but, although, yet, whereas, despite |
| Cause | because, due to, as a result, driven by, led to |
| Condition | if, unless, provided that, only if |
| Limit | only, except, solely, at least, no more than |
| Uncertainty | may, could, likely, suggests, expected, estimated |

A sentence with a signal word is worth more than three descriptive sentences: that is where the test builds its traps.

sections.h: Keyword matching: the statement first, then the text
sections.body:
For each statement:

1. **Extract 2-3 “rare” keywords**: proper names, numbers, dates, technical terms. Avoid generic words such as “company” or “market”, which appear everywhere.
2. **Use the map** to go to the right paragraph and look for the keywords by eye (scanning), without reading line by line.
3. **Read the sentence you found in full**, plus the one before and the one after if they contain a signal word.
4. **Apply the True / False / Cannot Say rule** from the previous lesson.

**Watch out for paraphrases**: the test almost always rewrites the text with synonyms. Look for the concept, not the exact word.

| In the passage | In the statement |
|---|---|
| turnover, sales | revenue |
| cut, trim, scale back | reduce |
| the six months to December | the second half (if the financial year runs from January to December) |
| headcount | number of employees |
| more than doubled | increased by over 100% |

sections.h: Same word does not mean same meaning
sections.body:
The most costly trap of keyword matching: you find the same words as in the statement and answer True on instinct. Tests deliberately build statements that reuse the words of the text while changing their meaning:

- **Negation or contrast**: “Contrary to forecasts of a 5% decline, income rose 3%” contains “5%” and “decline”, but says the opposite.
- **Swapped subject**: the text says that A acquired B, the statement that B acquired A.
- **Exception**: “all subsidiaries except the Brazilian one” is not the same as “all subsidiaries”.
- **Forecast presented as fact**: “analysts forecast X” does not mean that X happened.

**Rule**: when you find the match, slow down for 5 seconds and reread the **whole** sentence, especially the words that come before the match (contrary to, except, unlike, despite).

- **Cap per statement**: if after about 75 seconds you have not decided, choose the most likely answer and move on. The time lost on one question is paid for on three others.
- **Reasoned default**: if you hesitate between True and Cannot Say, ask yourself whether an assumption is needed; if so, Cannot Say. If you hesitate between False and Cannot Say, ask yourself whether you can point to the sentence that contradicts; if not, Cannot Say.
- **Do not leave answers blank**: in most online tests a wrong answer does not lose points, but always check the initial instructions.
- **Do not go back to answers already given**, except for obvious mistakes: the first rigorous analysis is usually the right one.

sections.h: How to train at the weekend
sections.body:
Speed is built with short, repeated exercises, not with marathons:

1. **10 minutes of active reading**: a business article in English (the companies or markets section of a financial newspaper). For each paragraph, write a 2-3 word label.
2. **Create your own statements**: for each article write 3 statements, one True, one False and one Cannot Say. Building the traps teaches you to recognise them.
3. **Timed sets**: do the sets on this site with the timer on and, for each error, note the cause (misleading keyword, assumption, outside knowledge, time).
4. **Error review**: after 3-4 sessions you will see that your errors concentrate on 1-2 causes. Work on those.

examples.q: Passage extract: Alvona Foods' financial year runs from January to December. Although turnover in Europe rose over the full year, it declined in the six months to December. Statement: Alvona's European sales fell in the second half of its financial year.
steps: Rare keywords in the statement: Alvona, European, second half (“sales” and “fell” are generic: look for their synonyms).
“Europe” leads to the second sentence; “sales” is paraphrased as “turnover”.
With a January to December financial year, “the six months to December” is the second half; “declined” is equivalent to “fell”.
The signal word “Although” separates the full year (growth) from the second half (decline): the statement concerns only the second half, so it is proved.

examples.q: Passage extract: Contrary to analysts' forecasts of a 5% decline, the bank's net interest income rose 3% in the quarter. Statement: The bank's net interest income fell 5% in the quarter.
steps: The keywords “net interest income”, “5%” and “quarter” are all in the same sentence: an apparently perfect match.
Rereading the whole sentence, “Contrary to” indicates that the 5% decline was only a forecast, contradicted by the facts.
The actual figure is +3%, incompatible with a 5% decline.

examples.q: Passage extract: All subsidiaries, except the Brazilian one, met their 2025 cash-flow targets. Statement: Every subsidiary met its 2025 cash-flow target.
steps: Keywords: subsidiary, 2025, cash-flow target: all in the same sentence.
The limit word “except” excludes the Brazilian subsidiary.
The text implies that the Brazilian subsidiary did not meet its target, so “every subsidiary” is contradicted.

examples.q: Passage extract: Headcount at the Milan office more than doubled between 2022 and 2025, while the London office was reorganised. Statement: The London office had fewer employees in 2025 than in 2022.
steps: The keyword “employees” corresponds to “headcount”, but in the text that figure concerns only Milan.
For London the text says only “was reorganised”: a reorganisation implies neither a decrease nor an increase in staff.
No sentence proves or contradicts the statement.

cheatsheet: A single read of the passage, with one label per paragraph.
Read the statement first and extract 2-3 rare keywords.
Look for the concept, not the word: tests paraphrase.
Once you find the match, reread the whole sentence and the nearby signal words.
Contrast, exception, uncertainty: that is where the traps hide.
Cap of about 75 seconds per statement, then decide.
Torn between True and Cannot Say: is an assumption needed? Then Cannot Say.
Do not leave answers blank, unless the instructions say otherwise.

lessons.title: Deductive reasoning: syllogisms, conditionals and ordering puzzles
lessons.summary: You will be able to establish whether a conclusion really follows from the premises, translate if / only if / unless without errors and solve ordering and seating puzzles with a diagram.

sections.body:
In deductive reasoning you receive some **premises** and one or more **conclusions**. You must say whether the conclusion **necessarily follows**: if the premises are true, the conclusion cannot be false.

Three principles:

- **Only the premises count**. A conclusion that is true in the real world but not guaranteed by the premises **does not follow**.
- **“Necessarily” is the key word**. A single case compatible with the premises in which the conclusion is false is enough to reject it.
- **Distinguish the type of question**: “must be true” (true in all possible cases), “could be true” (true in at least one case), “cannot be true” (false in all cases).

sections.h: Syllogisms: the four forms and the patterns
sections.body:
Each premise has one of four forms: **All A are B**, **No A are B**, **Some A are B**, **Some A are not B**.

| Premises | Valid conclusion |
|---|---|
| All A are B; All B are C | All A are C |
| All A are B; No B are C | No A are C |
| Some A are B; All B are C | Some A are C |
| No A are B; Some C are A | Some C are not B |
| No A are B | No B are A (can be reversed) |
| Some A are B | Some B are A (can be reversed) |

| Premises | Typical error (does NOT follow) |
|---|---|
| All A are B | All B are A |
| All A are B; All C are B | All A are C, or Some A are C |
| Some A are B; Some B are C | Some A are C |
| Some A are B | Some A are not B |
| All A are B; No A are C | No B are C |

In tests it is usually assumed that the sets are not empty: from “All A are B” you can conclude “Some A are B”.

When a syllogism does not fit the patterns, do not try to prove it: **try to break it**.

1. Draw the premises as circles (Venn diagram) **in the way least favourable** to the conclusion.
2. If you can build a case in which all the premises are true and the conclusion is false, the conclusion **does not follow**.
3. If every possible drawing makes the conclusion true, the conclusion **follows**.

**Quick trick**: replace A, B, C with concrete categories. “All cats are animals; all dogs are animals; therefore all cats are dogs” makes the error obvious in two seconds.

**Middle term rule**: the term that appears in both premises must be taken “in full” at least once, i.e. it must appear as the subject of a sentence with All or No, or as the predicate of a sentence with No or “are not”. If this never happens, the conclusion does not follow.

sections.h: Conditionals: translating if, only if, unless
sections.body:
Before reasoning, **rewrite every sentence in the form “if P then Q” (P → Q)**. P is the sufficient condition, Q the necessary one.

| Sentence in the test | Translation |
|---|---|
| If P, then Q | P → Q |
| P only if Q | P → Q |
| Only if Q, P | P → Q |
| Q is necessary for P | P → Q |
| P is sufficient for Q | P → Q |
| No P without Q | P → Q |
| All P are Q | P → Q |
| P unless Q | not Q → P (equivalent to: not P → Q) |
| P if and only if Q | P → Q and Q → P |

**Only if** is the main trap: “A deal is approved only if the committee signs off” says that the sign-off is **necessary**, not that it is enough. If the committee signs off, the deal **can** be approved, but it is not guaranteed.

**Unless** means “if not”: “The deal will close unless regulators object” = if the regulators do not object, the deal closes. It does **not** say what happens if the regulators object.

Given P → Q:

| You know that... | Can you conclude? | Name |
|---|---|---|
| P | Yes: Q | modus ponens |
| not Q | Yes: not P | modus tollens (contrapositive) |
| Q | No, P remains uncertain | affirming the consequent |
| not P | No, Q remains uncertain | denying the antecedent |

**Contrapositive**: P → Q is always equivalent to not Q → not P, never to Q → P. It is the most powerful tool in the test.

**Chains**: P → Q and Q → R give P → R. Line up the sentences so that the consequent of one is the antecedent of the next, using contrapositives when needed.

**Useful negations**:

- The negation of “all A are B” is “some A are not B” (not “no A are B”, which is a stronger statement).
- The negation of “some A are B” is “no A are B”.
- The negation of “if P then Q” is “P and not Q”.

Examples: five people presenting in sequence, deals closed on different days, analysts ranked by hours worked.

1. **Draw the slots** (1 2 3 4 5) and fix the direction (1 = first, highest, earliest).
2. **Insert the fixed clues**: “T presents third”, “E was not first”.
3. **Then the blocks**: “Q immediately after P” becomes a rigid block **PQ** that occupies two adjacent slots.
4. **Then the relations**: “R before S” becomes R < S. Join them into chains (T < R < S) when possible.
5. **If ambiguity remains, open the cases**: try the 2-3 possible positions of the most constrained block and eliminate those that violate a clue.
6. **Answer the right question**: “must be true” must hold in **all** the remaining cases, “could be true” in **at least one**.

Careful: “before” does not mean “immediately before”, and “not last” does not mean “first”.

**Straight-line table**: like ordering, but with right and left. Clarify the point of view: if the people are facing you, their right is your left.

**Round table**:

- **Fix one person** in any seat, preferably at the bottom of the drawing: in a circle only relative position counts, so you eliminate all equivalent rotations.
- **Left and right**: everyone is assumed to face the centre. For the person at the bottom of the drawing, their left coincides with your left on the page. For the person at the top, who is facing you, it is the opposite.
- **Opposite** exists only with an even number of seats: with 6 seats, the person opposite is 3 seats away.
- **Next to** does not say which side: open two cases.

Order of insertion: fixed person → “opposite” and “immediately left / right” clues → prohibitions (“not next to”) → remaining seats.

- Using real-world knowledge instead of the premises alone.
- Reversing a conditional: concluding Q → P from P → Q.
- Reading “only if” as “if”.
- Reading “unless” as “if and only if not”.
- Treating “before” as “immediately before”.
- Answering “must be true” to something that holds in only one of the possible cases.
- Not drawing: in your head you can get even a simple puzzle wrong. Always keep pen and paper next to the computer, if the test rules allow it.

examples.q: Premises: All analysts in the M&A team are CFA candidates. Some CFA candidates work at weekends. Conclusion: Some analysts in the M&A team work at weekends. Does the conclusion follow?
steps: Form: All A are B; Some B are C; proposed conclusion: Some A are C.
Middle term B (CFA candidates): it is the predicate of a sentence with All and the subject of a sentence with Some, so it is never taken in full.
Counterexample: all the M&A analysts are inside the set of CFA candidates, but those who work at weekends all belong to other teams. Premises true, conclusion false.
examples.answer: No, the conclusion does not follow.

examples.q: The bond will be repaid at par unless the issuer defaults. The bond was not repaid at par. Which statement must be true? (A) The issuer defaulted. (B) The issuer did not default. (C) The bond was repaid early. (D) It cannot be determined.
steps: Translate “unless”: if the issuer does not default → repayment at par.
You know that the bond was not repaid at par: this is the negation of the consequent.
Modus tollens (contrapositive): not repaid at par → the issuer defaulted.
Note: if instead you were told that the issuer defaulted, you could conclude nothing about the repayment.

examples.q: Five analysts, A, B, C, D and E, finish a model in a different order (1st to 5th). B finished before D. A finished immediately after C. E was neither first nor last. D was not last. Who finished last, and who must have finished first?
steps: Who can be last? Not E and not D (direct clues), not B (must come before D), not C (A finishes immediately after C). Only A remains: A = 5th.
The CA block forces C = 4th.
B, D and E occupy positions 1-3, with B before D and E not first. First is not E and cannot be D (B comes before it), so B = 1st.
Two cases remain: B, E, D or B, D, E. “B is first” is must be true; “D is second” is only could be true.
examples.answer: A is last; B is certainly first (and C is fourth).

examples.q: Six colleagues, Anna, Ben, Carla, Dario, Elena and Fabio, sit equally spaced around a round table, facing the centre. Anna sits directly opposite Dario. Ben sits immediately to Anna's left. Elena sits immediately to Dario's right. Carla does not sit next to Anna. Who sits directly opposite Ben?
steps: Fix Anna at the bottom. She faces the centre just as you do, so her left is your left on the page: Ben goes bottom left.
Dario is opposite Anna, so at the top. Dario is facing you, so his right is your left: Elena goes top left.
The two seats on the right remain: top right and bottom right. The bottom-right seat is next to Anna, so Carla goes top right and Fabio bottom right.
Opposite Ben (bottom left) is the top-right seat: Carla.

cheatsheet: A conclusion follows only if it is true in all cases compatible with the premises.
Middle term never taken in full (subject of All / No, predicate of No / are not) = invalid syllogism.
P only if Q = P → Q: Q is necessary, not sufficient.
P unless Q = if not Q, then P; it says nothing about what happens if Q.
P → Q is equivalent to not Q → not P, never to Q → P.
Negation of all = some ... not; negation of some = none.
Ordering: fixed clues, then blocks, then relations, then cases.
Round table: fix one person; everyone faces the centre.
Must be true = in all cases; could be true = in at least one.

lessons.title: Inductive and abstract reasoning: the rules checklist
lessons.summary: You will be able to break a sequence of figures down into independent elements and find the rules by testing a fixed checklist, instead of waiting for intuition.

sections.body:
In inductive tests (also called diagrammatic or abstract reasoning) the figures follow hidden rules. The most common formats:

- **Next in series**: 4-5 frames in sequence; choose the next one.
- **Odd one out**: find the figure that does not follow the rule of the others.
- **3×3 matrix**: one cell is missing; the rules apply across rows and/or columns.
- **Set A / Set B**: two groups with different rules; you assign a new figure to the right group or to neither.

Time is tight (often 45-75 seconds per item) and the figures almost always contain **2-3 simultaneous rules**. Those who wait for intuition get stuck; those who follow a checklist find the rules one at a time.

1. **Break it down**: list the elements present (e.g. “a circle, an arrow, some small squares”). Each element can have its own rule.
2. **Follow one element at a time** across all the frames, ignoring the others.
3. **Test the checklist** on that element until you find a rule that holds for **all** the frames, not just the first two.
4. **Predict the answer before looking at the options**, then eliminate every option that violates even a single rule.

If two options survive, you are missing a rule: go back to step 2 with the element that distinguishes those two options. The options themselves tell you which element matters.

| Rule | What to check | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Position | the element moves a fixed number of places (corners, cells, sides) | the dot moves on one corner clockwise |
| Rotation | constant angle and direction (45°, 90°, 180°) | the arrow rotates 90° clockwise |
| Colour / fill | black, grey, white, hatching; cycle or alternation | the circle alternates grey and white |
| Number | quantity of shapes, sides, lines, dots, intersections | +1 small square in each frame |
| Size | grows, shrinks, alternates | the triangle shrinks every two frames |
| Alternation | different rules in odd and even frames | odd frames with shapes, even frames with lines |
| Arithmetic progression | a quantity grows by a constant step, or the step itself grows | sides 3, 4, 5, 6: triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon |
| Superimposition | the third frame is the sum of the first two; the common parts disappear or remain | the lines present in both disappear |
| Symmetry / reflection | axis of symmetry; figure mirrored instead of rotated | the letter F becomes its mirror image |

**Recommended test order**: number → position → rotation → colour → size → alternation → progressions and superimpositions. The first four solve most standard items.

Do not simulate ten steps by eye: calculate.

- **Position**: if an element has N positions on a closed path (4 corners, the 8 border cells of a 3×3 grid) and moves k positions per frame, after n steps it has moved k × n positions. Divide by N and look at the remainder. Careful: from frame 1 to frame m there are **m − 1 steps**, not m.
- **Rotation**: angle after n steps = initial angle + step × n, minus multiples of 360°.
- **Colour cycle**: with a cycle of 3 colours, the colour of frame n depends on the remainder of (n − 1) divided by 3.

**Rotation or reflection?** An asymmetric figure (an F, a small flag, an arrow with a tick on one side) reveals the difference: rotated, it stays the same figure; mirrored, it switches side. Wrong options often use the mirror image.

sections.h: Odd one out, matrices and sets A / B
sections.body:
- **Odd one out**: find a property shared by all the figures but one. Test the checklist **by comparing the figures with each other**, not in sequence. Often the rule links two attributes (e.g. number of dots = number of sides − 2). If you find two rules that isolate different figures, choose the one that explains all the figures most simply.
- **3×3 matrices**: look for the rule first across the rows, then down the columns. Typical rules: each row contains each shape or colour once; the third cell is the sum or superimposition of the first two; a quantity grows along the row.
- **Set A / Set B**: find the feature **present in all** the figures in A and absent from all those in B (and vice versa). Often a new figure can belong to A, to B or to **neither**: do not forget the third option.

- **First 15 seconds**: break down and count.
- **Up to 45 seconds**: checklist on the most obvious element, then on the others.
- **At 60-75 seconds**: eliminate options with the rules already found and choose among those remaining. Often two rules out of three are enough to leave a single option.
- **Do not go back**: inductive items do not become easier on a second look, but the other questions do.

In practice, after each error write down **which rule on the checklist you did not test**. Within a few sessions you will see your recurring blind spot (usually counting sides or confusing rotation with reflection).

examples.q: A square has a dot in one corner. Frame 1: the dot is black, in the top-left corner. In each new frame the dot moves one corner clockwise and its colour alternates (black, white, black, white...). What does frame 6 show?
steps: Two independent rules: position (one corner clockwise) and colour (alternation).
Position: from frame 1 to frame 6 there are 5 steps; 5 divided by 4 corners leaves a remainder of 1, so one corner on from top-left, clockwise: top-right.
Colour: odd frames black, even frames white; 6 is even, so white.
Prediction: a white dot in the top right. Eliminate any option with the dot black or in another corner.
examples.answer: A white dot in the top-right corner.

examples.q: Frame 1: an arrow inside a circle points up, the circle is grey and there is 1 small square outside the circle. In each new frame the arrow rotates 90° clockwise, the circle alternates grey and white, and one small square is added. Which option is frame 5? (A) Arrow up, white circle, 5 squares (B) Arrow left, grey circle, 5 squares (C) Arrow up, grey circle, 5 squares (D) Arrow up, grey circle, 4 squares
steps: Rotation: from frame 1 to frame 5 there are 4 steps; 4 × 90° = 360°, so the arrow points up again. Eliminate B.
Colour: odd frames grey; 5 is odd, so grey. Eliminate A.
Number: 1 + 4 = 5 small squares. Eliminate D.
C remains, which respects all three rules.
examples.answer: C. Arrow up, grey circle, 5 squares.

examples.q: Which figure is the odd one out? (A) A hexagon with 4 dots inside (B) A triangle with 2 dots inside (C) A square with 2 dots inside (D) A heptagon with 5 dots inside (E) A pentagon with 3 dots inside
steps: The shapes and the number of dots all change: the rule must link two attributes.
Compare sides and dots: hexagon 6 and 4, square 4 and 2, heptagon 7 and 5, pentagon 5 and 3. In every case dots = sides − 2.
Triangle: 3 − 2 = 1 dot expected, but it has 2.
B is the only figure that violates the rule.

cheatsheet: Break the figure down into elements and follow one element at a time.
Checklist: number, position, rotation, colour, size, alternation, progression, superimposition, reflection.
Expect 2-3 simultaneous rules.
Predict the answer before looking at the options, then eliminate.
Position after n steps (frame m = m − 1 steps): movement k × n, then the remainder of the division by the number of positions.
Rotation after n steps: step × n, minus multiples of 360°.
If nothing seems to change, count sides, lines, intersections, angles.
Rotated or mirrored? Check an asymmetric detail.
Set A / B: always consider the “neither” option too.

lessons.title: Number and letter series: the differences method
lessons.summary: You will be able to solve number and letter series with a fixed sequence of checks (differences, ratios, interleaved series, known series) in under a minute.

sections.body:
Series appear in numerical and logical reasoning tests and also in inductive tests, where the counts in the figures become numbers. A series can be solved in 20-40 seconds if you know **in what order to look**; minutes are lost if you try to guess.

The golden rule: **a rule is valid only if it explains all the terms**, not just the first three.

1. **Look at the trend**: does it grow slowly (sums), quickly (products or powers), or go up and down (two interleaved series or alternating operations)?
2. **First differences**: write the difference between consecutive terms under the series. If it is constant, you are done.
3. **Second differences**: if the first differences are not constant, calculate their differences. They are often constant or form a simple series.
4. **Ratios**: if the series grows fast, divide each term by the previous one (×2, ×3, or ×2 + 1).
5. **Odd and even positions**: if nothing works, separate the terms in odd positions from those in even positions: they are often two independent series.
6. **Known series**: squares, cubes, prime numbers, Fibonacci (each term is the sum of the two previous ones).

sections.h: Catalogue of the most frequent patterns
sections.body:
| Pattern | Example | Next term |
|---|---|---|
| Constant difference | 7, 11, 15, 19 | 23 |
| Increasing differences | 3, 5, 9, 15, 23 (+2, +4, +6, +8) | 33 |
| Constant ratio | 3, 6, 12, 24 | 48 |
| ×a + b | 3, 7, 15, 31 (×2 + 1) | 63 |
| Alternating operations | 2, 6, 7, 21, 22 (×3, +1) | 66 |
| Two interleaved series | 4, 20, 7, 17, 10, 14 (+3 on odd positions, −3 on even positions) | 13 |
| Fibonacci | 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 | 21 |
| Squares ± k | 2, 5, 10, 17, 26 (n² + 1) | 37 |
| Cubes | 1, 8, 27, 64 | 125 |
| Prime numbers | 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 | 17 |
| Differences = prime numbers | 1, 3, 6, 11, 18 (+2, +3, +5, +7) | 29 |

sections.h: Letter series: turn them into numbers
sections.body:
Convert each letter into its position in the English alphabet (26 letters) and solve the number series.

| Letter | E | J | O | T | Y |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Position | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 |

Memorise **EJOTY** (the multiples of 5): from there you count at most two letters forwards or backwards.

Other tools:

- **Reverse position**: A ↔ Z, B ↔ Y, C ↔ X. The sum of the two positions is always 27 (A = 1, Z = 26).
- **Wrapping round the alphabet**: after Z you start again from A. If you get 28, subtract 26: 28 − 26 = 2 = B.
- **Letter groups**: in “AZ, CX, EV, ?” the first letter moves forward by 2 (A, C, E, G) and the second moves back by 2 (Z, X, V, T): answer GT.
- **The English alphabet includes J, K, W, X, Y**, letters rarely used in Italian: skipping them is a frequent mistake.

- **Number + letter**: in “2B, 4D, 8H, ?” the numbers double (2, 4, 8, 16) and the letter corresponds to the number (B = 2, D = 4, H = 8, P = 16): answer 16P.
- **Fractions**: treat the numerator and the denominator as two separate series.
- **Decreasing series**: the same rules apply in reverse (÷2, −3, shrinking differences).
- **Missing term in the middle**: use the terms **on both sides** of the gap to check the rule.
- **Wrong term** (“which number does not fit?”): find the rule on at least four terms, then identify the only one that violates it.

- **Stopping at the first three terms**: 2, 4, 8 can continue with 16 (×2) or with 14 (differences +2, +4, +6). Always check against the whole series.
- **Ignoring interleaved series**: if the series goes up and down, there are almost always two alternating series or two alternating operations.
- **Getting the position of the requested term wrong**: in an interleaved series, does the missing term belong to the odd or the even subseries? Count the positions.
- **Errors with letters**: write the position under each letter; do not count in your head.
- **Time**: if after 45 seconds you do not have the rule, work from the options: calculate the difference between the last term and each option; often only one is compatible with the trend of the differences.

examples.q: What comes next? 4, 9, 18, 31, 48, ?
steps: First differences: 9 − 4 = 5, 18 − 9 = 9, 31 − 18 = 13, 48 − 31 = 17: not constant.
Second differences: 9 − 5 = 4, 13 − 9 = 4, 17 − 13 = 4: constant.
Next first difference: 17 + 4 = 21.
Next term: 48 + 21 = 69.

examples.q: What comes next? 5, 10, 7, 14, 11, 22, ?
steps: The series goes up and down: suspect alternating operations.
The next step is −3: 22 − 3 = 19.
Very different terms and a zigzag trend: separate odd and even positions.
The missing term is the 8th, so an even one: 40 − 5 = 35.

examples.q: What comes next? C, F, J, O, ?
steps: Convert: C = 3, F = 6, J = 10, O = 15.
Differences: +3, +4, +5, so the next is +6.
15 + 6 = 21. From T = 20 (EJOTY) move forward one letter: U.

cheatsheet: Order: trend → first differences → second differences → ratios → odd / even → known series.
A rule holds only if it explains all the terms.
Zigzag = two interleaved series or alternating operations.
Rapid growth = multiplication, ×a + b or powers.
Letters: convert them into numbers, A = 1, Z = 26.
Reverse position: the sum is 27 (A ↔ Z).
Beyond Z: subtract 26 and start again from A.

lessons.title: Work style and personality questionnaires
lessons.summary: You will understand how personality questionnaires are used in graduate programmes and how to answer sincerely, consistently and in line with the role, including in forced-choice formats.

sections.h: What they are and how banks use them
sections.body:
Many selection processes add to the cognitive tests a questionnaire on how you work: preferences, behaviours, motivations. There are no right or wrong answers in absolute terms, but the result is compared with the **role profile**, i.e. the competencies the bank considers important for an analyst.

Typical uses:

- **Fit score**: a profile very far from the desired one can weigh on the decision, especially if the cognitive test results are borderline.
- **Interview guide**: the extreme points of your profile become questions (“the questionnaire says you prefer working alone: tell me about a time you worked in a team under pressure”).
- **Development**: after hiring, it is sometimes used in training programmes.

Exactly how it is used varies from bank to bank and is almost never public: preparing means being consistent, not guessing an algorithm.

| Format | How it works | What it measures well |
|---|---|---|
| Likert scale | you rate a statement from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” | the intensity of each trait |
| Forced choice | in a block of 3-4 statements you choose the one most and the one least like you | priorities between traits; harder to “inflate” |
| Ranking | you order 3-4 statements from most to least like you | like forced choice, with more detail |
| Strengths-based | you rate how much energy an activity gives you, sometimes with a time limit | motivation and natural strengths |

In forced-choice formats the statements in a block are usually **equally desirable**: you cannot choose “the right one”; you have to reveal what comes first for you.

Before the test, be clear about which behaviours a banking graduate programme looks for. For analyst roles (IB, markets, corporate banking, risk) these come up almost every time:

| Area | Typical behaviours |
|---|---|
| Reliability | accuracy, checking for errors, meeting deadlines |
| Resilience | calm under pressure, variable workloads, response to feedback |
| Drive | ambition, eagerness to learn, initiative |
| Teamwork | collaboration, supporting colleagues, clear communication |
| Integrity | following the rules, transparency about mistakes |
| Client focus | listening, quality of service, attention to needs |
| Analytical thinking | working with data, structured reasoning |

Also read the **values published by the bank** on its careers page: they are often 4-5 words that you will find again in the questionnaire, in the situational judgement tests and in the interview questions.

sections.h: Answering sincerely but in line with the role
sections.body:
The right strategy is not to lie: a profile constructed on paper collapses at interview and at the assessment centre. It is about **presenting the authentic version of yourself at work**, in the context of the role.

1. **Answer thinking of yourself at work or in your studies**, not in your private life. “I enjoy routine” at work can mean something different from at the weekend.
2. **Think about behaviours, not intentions**: what have you actually done in the last year, at a bank or at university?
3. **On the traits central to the role** (accuracy, resilience, teamwork, integrity), if they are true of you, answer decisively: “agree” or “strongly agree”.
4. **Avoid systematically choosing the middle**: too many “neutral” answers produce a flat profile that says nothing about you. It is a typical risk for those who tend towards modesty.
5. **Avoid extremes everywhere**: “strongly agree” on every positive trait looks like an attempt to appear perfect.
6. **Pace**: 8-15 seconds per statement. The first considered answer is usually the most authentic.

The questionnaire measures each trait with **several statements**, worded in different ways and spread across the test. Some are **reversed**:

- “I always check my work before submitting it.”
- “I sometimes submit work without reviewing it when I am busy.”

If you answer “strongly agree” to both, your profile comes out inconsistent. Many questionnaires calculate a **consistency index** and some include social desirability statements (“I have never made a mistake at work”), to which almost nobody can sincerely answer “strongly agree”.

How to stay consistent:

- Read each statement to the end: “not”, “rarely”, “sometimes” reverse its direction.
- Anchor your answers to real examples: if you have a concrete episode in mind, you will answer the same way every time.
- Align the profile with your CV and with what you will say at interview.

You receive a block of statements, all of them positive, and must choose **most like me** and **least like me**.

1. **Read the statements** and assign a trait to each one (accuracy, sociability, creativity, resilience...).
2. **Sincerity filter**: exclude from “most” anything that is not true of you.
3. **Role filter**: among the true statements, for “most” choose the one most central to an analyst's job.
4. **For “least”** choose the one least characteristic of you **and** least critical for the role. Never put a key trait (e.g. integrity or accuracy) in “least” unless it really is your weak point.
5. **Consistency across blocks**: the same trait comes back in different blocks paired with others; keep the same order of priority.

Forced choice makes you reveal an order, and that is not a bad thing: an analyst who puts accuracy above being the centre of attention is credible.

- Write down 5-6 traits of the role and, next to each one, a real example of your own.
- Reread the bank's values.
- Take the test rested and without interruptions: even if it is not timed, tiredness increases inconsistent answers.
- Do not give the same answer to entire blocks of statements.
- After the test, note the traits on which you answered at the extremes and prepare an example for each one: they may come up again at interview.

examples.q: Statement: I double-check figures before sending a document, even when I am under time pressure. (Strongly disagree / Disagree / Neutral / Agree / Strongly agree)
steps: Trait measured: accuracy and reliability, central for an analyst.
Sincerity check: do you really do it? Think of a concrete episode in which you checked a model or a pitch against a deadline.
If so, answer Agree or Strongly agree and keep the same position on similar statements (and the opposite one on reversed statements).
examples.answer: Agree or Strongly agree, if it matches your actual behaviour; then stay consistent on similar items.

examples.q: Choose the statement MOST like you and the one LEAST like you: (A) I stay calm when a deadline is brought forward unexpectedly. (B) I enjoy being the centre of attention at social events. (C) I make sure every number in my work can be traced to a source. (D) I like trying unconventional approaches to problems.
steps: Traits: A resilience, B social extroversion, C accuracy, D creativity.
Role filter: A and C are central for an analyst; D is useful but secondary; B is of little relevance.
Most: between A and C, choose the one that is truer of you (e.g. C, if making every number traceable is your standard in M&A models).
Least: B, if it really reflects your preferences; do not put A or C in least just for variety.
examples.answer: Most: C (or A); Least: B, if consistent with your actual behaviour.

examples.q: Item 12: I always finish tasks I have started. Item 47: I sometimes leave tasks unfinished when something more interesting comes up. A candidate answers Strongly agree to both. What is the problem, and how should they answer?
steps: The two statements measure the same trait (perseverance) in opposite directions: item 47 is reversed.
Strongly agree to both is logically inconsistent and lowers the consistency index.

A consistent answer, if you usually finish your tasks: Agree to item 12 and Disagree to item 47. With an absolute such as “always”, Agree is more credible than Strongly agree if you admit some exceptions.
examples.answer: Inconsistency between a direct item and a reversed item; consistent answer: Agree to 12, Disagree to 47.

cheatsheet: There are no right answers, but there is a role profile.
Answer as you are at work, based on real behaviours.
Central traits for an analyst: accuracy, resilience, drive, teamwork, integrity.
No systematic neutrals, no strongly agree everywhere.
Watch out for reversed items: not, rarely, sometimes.
Forced choice: sincerity first, then relevance to the role.
Never put a key trait in least unless it really is your weak point.
Your profile comes back at interview: prepare an example for every extreme answer.
